review:
First things first: This game was originally called Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis, it was ranamed Arma due to legal problems between publishers and developers.

Now to the review:
I came across Operation Flashpoint way back on 2001. It was just mind blowing, at that point there simply were no game with such an broad scope and such a powerful imersion.

The story takes place in the good´n old 80´s, when there were real intenational tension and warfare wasn´t a matter of eletronics, laser targeting and remote vehicles.
A crazy russian general takes a nuke, a division of the red army and a lot of tanks and takes over some islands in the north atlantic, but those islands are under NATO protection, so the war begins.

During the game you take the role of 4 soldier with distinct roles in the army. A foot soldier, a tank pilot, a chopper pilot and a black ops expert. With all 4 you climb up in the ranks, starting as a grunt and ending up in commanding large groups of units on the battlefield. It also ends in delivering a very diverse experience, as you play on several unique missions and control an interesting variety of ground and air vehicles.

The gameplay is rather chunky, the movement is very limited, it all seems weird at first, but it is actually very immersive. There is one of the great virtues of the game, its realistic aproach to combined arms warfare. If you imagine that a soldier is carrying over 20kgs of equipment and ammo, it would be really hard to run and jump as you do in Call of Duty.
Without planning and the right resources, there´s nothing a squad of soldiers can do agains an armored vehicle, and the importance of air support is acurately shown.
The game is very unforgiving, the damage system works like this: Shot in the legs, and you can´t stand. Shot in the arms, you cant aim. Shot twice and you die. Shot in the head, game over.
This actually works out very well, as this system forces the player to play cautiously, and adopt real world strategies to stay alive. You are forced to take cover, to look around for enemies before moving, to pay attention to orders and intel in order to not fall in a trap or get flanked.

Another strong point from this game is the support developers gave to the community. The game was designed to be easily modded, and the developers were very active in the community, patching the game and implementing features that the players asked for.
The game also featured an mission editor mode, wich was the same used by the developers to create the main campaign, allowing players to create their own missions at will, sharing with other players or even creating awesome co-op or PvP missions.
It was a very new thing at the time, and the community was very solid. This philosophy is still kind of rare, but it was always part of the Arma series, and Arma 3 specifically targets for a relevant community participation in game developing and content creation.


Operation Flashpoint was improved in nearly every aspect along the Arma series, but still stands as the game that started it all.

Its vast open terrain, flexible and diverse gameplay, realistic aproach and some trully memorable events changed the landscape of the military games and still survives as an enjoiable game.

In it´s time it deserved a 10/10.

Today, we can see that it aged well, and still attracts attention as milestone in millitary simulation. 8/10

There was a time when life was wonderfully simple. My biggest worry wasn't deadlines, bills or responsibilities. It was making sure my squad survived another mission in Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis.

I spent countless afternoons and entire summer vacations lost in this game. I'd replay missions over and over, convinced that this time I'd save everyone. When I wasn't fighting through the campaign, I'd disappear into the mission editor for hours, creating my own battles, invasions and impossible last stands. Half of them were disasters. The other half existed only because a kid with a wild imagination believed he could direct his own war.

Back then, the world outside barely existed. It was just me, my PC, the sound of distant gunfire, and that unforgettable menu music welcoming me back every single day.

Loading up ARMA: Cold War Assault now feels less like launching a game and more like opening a forgotten photo album.

The blocky graphics. The stiff animations. The radio chatter I somehow still remember line for line. It all comes flooding back in an instant. For a few precious moments, I'm not an adult anymore. I'm that kid again, sitting in front of a bulky CRT monitor, completely immersed in a world that felt impossibly real.

People often say nostalgia makes old games seem better than they were. Maybe that's true sometimes. But Cold War Crisis was genuinely special. Long before realistic military shooters became popular, it trusted the player. Every firefight felt dangerous. Every mission demanded patience. Every victory felt earned because the game never held your hand.

It wasn't just teaching me how to play. Looking back, it quietly taught me patience, planning and that sometimes the best strategy was simply knowing when not to pull the trigger.

For those of us who grew up with it, this isn't just an old military simulator. It's a time capsule. A reminder of carefree afternoons that somehow disappeared without us noticing. Of racing home after school. Of endless weekends. Of mission editor experiments that crashed spectacularly. Of promising myself, "Just one more mission," until I looked outside and realized the sun had already set.

Some games entertain you.

A very small number become part of your childhood.

Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis became part of mine.

11/10. Because some games aren't measured in graphics or mechanics. They're measured in memories.

So many years after its release, it can be funny when you look at the technical side. But if you're able to look past that, it's still a fantastic game that can amaze you with very realistic and open gameplay as well as brilliant atmosphere.

This is one of the best games ever made! Although it came out in 2001, it is still not outdated, and I regularly play it in 2013. The reason why is because it has so much potential. First, there are two official campaigns, that take place in a possible Cold War conflict, which escalates into armed confrontation. You play either as a infantryman or a squad leader, but can also access any unoccupied land/sea/air vehicle should you need or want to. Every mission in this game in non-linear, so it offers unique experience each time you play it. Story is believable and takes a realistic approach towards waging a war (you are not always on the offensive - sometimes retreat can be regarded as a strategic success). In addition to that, there are many separate single missions that offer a new perspective on the original story. But the real benefit comes with tons of free addons, created by modders. That way, you can expand the game with countless new units, weapons, vehicles, missions and even campaigns if you want. Some are even total conversions, which improve graphics and gameplay mechanics too.

Speaking of wich, I have to mention that default gameplay mechanics appeal to me very much, especially looking around and aiming. In my opinion this game feels better and easier to play than its successors in the game series.
The only area that lacks a bit is AI driving. It can sometimes miss the road and break immersion, but otherwise it's ok.

But my favourite feature (that you should absolutely try) is mission editor. It is easy to use and combined with the previously mentioned addons, you can design and play in your own playground of destruction. You can instantly play your missions as you design them, so you can test different approaches and decide whether to actively participate in them or just be a mere observer. You can create massive battles with air, land and sea units or just small skirmishes to try different tactics. The only barrier is your imagination and I still haven't reached it in more than 10 years of experience.

I definitely recommend this game - its value far exceeds its price.

The year is 1997. Two brothers from Czech Republic, Ondřej and Marek Španěl, alongside their business partner Slavomír Pavlíček started working on a new game. The team had envisioned an open world realistic tactical shooter and so Poseidon entered development. Flash forward to year 1999. The three form a new game development studio titled Bohemia Interactive and Poseidon eventually gets released in 2001 as Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Rising, published by Codemasters.

Following it's massive success, Bohemia started working on so called "game 2", a sequel to Operation Flashpoint. However BI and Codemasters went separate ways after several conflicts and Codemasters kept the flashpoint licence. Eventually in 2005, Bohemia released a sequel to Operation Flashpoint, titled Arma: Armed Assault. It's massive success led BI to kickstart the Arma franchise as the official sequels to the original Operation Flashpoint. 
Inspired by their success, Codemasters followed and released two of their own Operation Flashpoint games, Red River and Dragon Rising. Their failure led Codemasters to abandon the franchise while Bohemia Interactive's Arma series thrived thanks to Arma 2.

In 2011, Bohemia signed an agreement with Codemasters and Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Rising was handed back to Bohemia Interactive, who re-released it digitally as Arma: Cold War Assault and so the series went full circle.


The game uses photoscanned textures and environments. While the models may look a bit blocky by 2001 standards, the textures hold up really well and the game also sports a good lighting system for the time and it also has a really nice visual style that holds a lot of magic. The sound design is pretty good for the time aswell, especially with the EAX sound system. The gunfire echoes realistically through the environment, the developers even coded sound travel time simulation, the gunshot sounds are meaty and the ambience is pretty good. The voice acting sounds a bit unnatural due to the way the voice lines are handled but this system also allows for a huge variety of different situational voice calls that very few games have even today.

The soundtrack is also pretty amazing. Composed by Ondřej Matejka, it is a combination of orchestral music and synths and feels like a 1980s action movie score. There are plenty of great and memorable tracks and it's definitely worth giving it a listen even outside the game.

What really sells this game though is it's unpreceeded attention to detail and raw realism. While it may not seem that advanced nowadays, it's pretty damn impressive for 2001. The maps are huge, have realistic terrain and a lot of small hidden details and easter eggs. You can use gas stations, climb up elevator shafts and so on. Since the game is set in 1985, it also faithfully replicates the atmosphere and feel of the 1980s with period accurate uniforms and weaponry (with the exception of the PP-19), vehicles etc.

You die in a few shots, there's a radio calls system and different soldier specialisations with different equipment and role. The levels are huge and very open aswell, allowing you to approach situations in a lot of unique ways. You can also drive a variety of vehicles and the game sports strong mod tools as well as a very nice mission editor. The game does feel a bit janky but you'll quickly get accustomed to the controls and gameplay. It's a hardcore shooter which requires you to tacticise and you cannot go in guns-blazing.

The main campaign takes place in 1985 and follows 4 main protagonists from the US Military: Corporal David Armstrong, Lieutenant Robert Hammer, Captain Sam Nichols and Captain James Gastowski fighting in an armed conflict on the Malden Islands against the Soviet Army. 
The Steam version also gets pre-packaged with the Resistance expansion where you play as Viktor Troska, a guerilla fighting against the Soviets on the island of Nogova three years prior to the events of the main campaign.
You get a nice variety of different missions on several different islands. The missions are unique, the storyline is cheesy but fun and memorable. 

 A second expansion titled Red Hammer also came out, but it was developed by a different studio and is non-canon.

Simply put
+ Soundtrack
+ Sound design

+ Graphics
+ Mission structure
+ Realism
+ Level Design

Simply a great game made by a passionate and small team from Czech Republic that deserves more recognition. If you've ever played any of the newer Arma games, make sure to get this one aswell to see how the franchise began back in 2001 and you'll definitely feel right at home here and get a lot of fun outta this one. This game is the father of the modern milsim genre and is definitely worth getting.

[b]It is the last mission... We've beaten the Russians off to the end of the island, and now it's time to apprehend the mastermind behind it all... [i]General Guba[/i].[/b]


Me and my spec ops team of eight finish our briefing: to find and capture General Guba alive before he makes his escape off the island. As we make for Guba's headquarters in our M113 Armored Personnel Carrier, we see a friendly machine gun jeep, probably forming into the friendly assault that will schedule a little while later. As we drive further to our objective, I spot a dirt trail along the mountain path. We follow it to find two ruskies guarding an abandoned outpost with a Mil Mi-24 [b]"Hind"[/b] attack chopper hiding in the back. The gunner of the M113 takes out the two in quick bursts and I tell my men to board the Hind. "Out of fuel" 3 in my squad tells me. I find a fuel truck hiding behind a wall and refuel the Hind. As we start the chopper me and my men get ready for what comes next...


As we fly our way to Guba's base, we evade enemy anti aircraft vehicles, namely the  ZSU-23-4 [b]"Shilka"[/b]. A little while later, we spot a friendly assault on the frontlines. An M113 supported by a group of infantry heads for Guba's base. A few yards beyond them, we see the diabolical ruskie tank, the [b]T-80[/b]. I tell my gunner to engage the T-80 before our friendlies get slaughtered. I hover the chopper for my gunner to lock on and we destroy the T-80 just in time before it fires a shot at the M113. As we see the friendly assault push forward, we return to our main objective.


We hover over Guba's base and spot him in a UAZ, getting ready to leave for good. Luckily we catch him before even sets a good distance into the Shilka infested lands. My gunner guns down any infantry and spetsnaz units guarding Guba and we land to apprehend him. As we finally apprehend the mastermind, he speaks in Russian of how the island will be nuked with his SCUD launchers that is set up somewhere on the opposite side of the island. Lucky for me, I can translate what he was saying and report it to command. Command replies that our new objective is to take out the SCUD launchers ASAP. As we board into the Hind once again along with our whimpering captive, we search for the SCUD launchers...


I hover around the coast and spot a group of Shilka AA vehicles firing at me. A little beyond, I spot the SCUD launchers... Ready to launch. I tell my gunner to fire at will at the Shilkas but we take too many hits. My gunner and a few others in my squad are dead... I tell my remaining men to ditch as our helicopter moves closer to the ground... crash landing...


Me and a few others, including the captive ditch the chopper just before we hit the ground. I find my legs bleeding and look at the crash site. I call all my units to report their positions to me. Only three of my men were left, along with our captive. I tell them to stay put and look after the captive. As I look infront of me, I see the SCUD launcher's nuclear warhead. I'm lucky to be so close to the nuke... but not so lucky to have my legs broken. As I crawl my way to the SCUD launcher, I spot the same ruskie Shilkas that shot down our chopper. Luckily they seem to be too trained to the skies in search of more prey. I was suprised at how there was not much infantry guarding the SCUD launchers. I crawl my way under the SCUD launchers and plant a satchel charge for each. I crawl my way back to the Hind crash site and tell command the job is done. I take a look back to the nuclear warheads. [i]I set off the charges and watch the explosion.[/i] [b]"Mission Complete".[/b]

Hands down, my favorite game in the world. I spent countless hours as a teenager playing this game. This game is one of the major contributing factors towards me joining the Marines when I was younger. Originally this game was called Operation Flashpoint. But then another company bought the rights to that name, and they made a bunch of crappy Operation Flashpoints after the firts. The original devs, no longer able to use the name Operation Flashpoint, started creating games called Arma, so all the Arma games that are extremely popular, including DayZ, came about because of this game. This game started it all. It was extremely advanced for it's time, probably one of the few realistic games out back then, and it holds up even with time. This game has incredible substance. Graphics are very dated, and many things are very dated indeed, but not the subtance and things to do in this game. Not to mention, one can download an extreme amount of mods for this game, really this is how I spent my time playing this game, with mods. 

If there is one mod I recommend over all overs, it's the Finnish Defense Forces mod. Has you playing as the Fins fighting an insurrection against the Soviets.

Again, if someone asked me which was my favorite video game, that got me into politics, war, history, etc. It would be this game.

The game that taught me the true meaning of "realism" in gaming. I mean, who needs a social life when you can spend hours trying to get a tank to move 5 feet without getting stuck in a ditch?

In all seriousness, ARMA: Cold War Assault is a game that will test your patience, your skills, and your sanity. But if you're up for the challenge, it can be incredibly rewarding. The game's attention to detail is impressive, with realistic military tactics and equipment that will make you feel like a real soldier (minus the whole "getting shot at" thing).

One of the things I loved about the game is the sense of immersion. The environments are beautifully rendered, and the sound design is top-notch. I found myself getting completely absorbed in the game world, even when I was stuck in a never-ending loop of "try to get tank unstuck, fail, repeat."

Of course, the game isn't without its flaws. The controls can be clunky at times, and the AI can be a bit wonky. But overall, I found that the game's strengths far outweigh its weaknesses.

So, would I recommend ARMA: Cold War Assault to others? Absolutely. But only if you're a glutton for punishment. If you're looking for a game that will challenge you, frustrate you, and maybe even make you cry a little (I'm not ashamed to admit it), then ARMA: Cold War Assault is the game for you.

ArmA: Cold War Assault (formerly known as Operation Flashpoint: Resistance) is a classic. It's a military simulation and first person shooter, designed to replicate with the experience of modern warfare on open battlefields. Keeping in mind that this game was originally released in 2001, it was technically extremely impressive at the time.

You can play virtually any role on the battlefield: from infantry soldier to squad commander, sabotaging enemy bases at night as part of your Spec Ops team, driving Jeeps, lorries and tanks, piloting jets and helicopters. You are not restricted to playing alongside NATO but can also fight in the Red Army or in the resistance factions. There are no maps as such, missions can be set on any of the 4 islands the game has to offer, each of them dozens of square miles/kilometres in size featuring villages, towns, mountains, forests, beaches and a road network to explore.

The core or the vanilla game is its lengthy campaign set in 1985 and depicts a direct confrontation between the US and Soviets on a fictional archipelago. The campaign is notoriously difficult, the enemy AI is very punishing and most missions give you a lot of freedom into deciding on how you aim to complete your objective. It's an extremely rewarding experience and it will gradually introduce you to all aspects of the game as you'll play through the eyes of 4 different characters.
The second campaign is a prequel set 3 years before the main events on a 40 sq mi/100 km2 island where you will play as part of the resistance. This campaign has even more depth and missions are not linear anymore as your actions can ripple through the next missions.

Graphics have aged a lot, the colour pallet feels a bit bland by today's standards (the ground seems to be a shade of green, beige or yellow) and the controls are not always intuitive (you need to use a small menu for most actions, aiming through an iron sight is achieved by pressing a key) but that's not what you will play this game.

You will play it because it paved the way for military simulations and makes you feel like you're an insignificant part of a much bigger conflict, because you can climb in any vehicle and explore the entire island if you want. Even if you are brave enough to complete both campaigns as well as all the single player missions, you will find thousands of mods, campaigns and missions online that push the boundaries of what this game can achieve. Nothing stops you from creating your own missions either thanks to the in-game editor.

ArmA: Cold War Assault is a masterpiece that offers a unique experience, it tests your patience and motivation but will reward you greatly for persevering.

Notes:
1- ArmA:CWA runs on any modern PC with no performance problem whatsoever. You can max out all graphics except for 2 parameters that I would recommend you to not touch: Visibility (set to 900) and Terrain detail (set to Normal). Pushing these values too high can make your game run extremely slow or crash (even if you have a powerful gaming PC) and the single player missions are usually not designed for high visibility which can cause some issues.
2- In 2002, Codemasters released an entire new campaign named Red Hammer, letting you play on the Soviet side. As BIS doesn't own the rights to it, it's not included. One way to install it is to find a legal copy of the expansion pack and copy the RedHammer.pbo from the CD to your campaigns folder. This campaign is very good as well and worth a try.

Arma: Cold War Assault stands as one of the most influential military simulators ever released, not because of modern polish or cinematic presentation, but because of how boldly it redefined what a tactical shooter could be. Developed and published by Bohemia Interactive, the game—originally known as Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis—places players in the middle of a fictional conflict between NATO and Soviet forces at the height of late-Cold War tension. Rather than funneling you through scripted corridors, it drops you into sprawling island battlefields where the terrain is vast, the stakes are high, and every mission feels like a small piece of a larger, unpredictable war.

The campaign offers a wide variety of roles, putting players in the boots of infantrymen, behind the controls of tanks, and even inside military helicopters. Each mission unfolds across kilometers of open countryside, forests, coastal villages, and mountain roads, making navigation, positioning, and awareness just as important as marksmanship. What sets Cold War Assault apart is its demand for patience and tactical thinking: firefights happen at long distances, ambushes are genuinely dangerous, and vehicles do not feel like flashy power-ups but essential tools to survive and maneuver in the field. The game’s emphasis on “combined arms” warfare—blending infantry, armor, and air support—was groundbreaking for its time and remains a core identity of the Arma series today.

The sense of realism extends beyond weapon handling and large maps. The game’s pacing is intentionally slower, favoring methodical progression over instant gratification. Missions rarely rely on predictable waves of enemies; instead, threats can emerge naturally from the world, elevating tension as you scan distant tree lines or listen for the rumble of approaching engines. The story, while understated, gains power through this grounded approach. The campaign’s protagonists feel like ordinary soldiers thrust into extraordinary circumstances, and the narrative—especially when paired with the Resistance expansion—captures the desperation, uncertainty, and sacrifice of war without melodrama.

Despite its enduring legacy, Cold War Assault does show its age. The interface and controls can feel stiff and unintuitive compared to modern shooters, and the animations and textures reflect the technical limitations of early 2000s hardware. The AI, though ambitious for its time, can behave erratically, causing moments of immersion to clash with moments of frustration. Close-quarters combat especially highlights these limitations, with movement and aiming feeling noticeably clunky. However, players willing to adjust to the older design will find a depth of simulation that few newer titles attempt, making its quirks more a matter of adaptation than deal-breakers.

One of the most impressive aspects of the game’s legacy is its mission editor and modding support. Even at release, Cold War Assault came with robust tools that allowed players to design entire scenarios, craft custom campaigns, and create new gameplay systems. This openness fostered a passionate community that extended the life of the game for years, contributing thousands of user-made missions and modifications. Many hallmarks of the modern Arma experience—sandbox scenarios, realism mods, experimental units—were shaped here, turning Cold War Assault into both a beloved game and a creative platform.

Arma: Cold War Assault remains a historic milestone in tactical gaming. It is not a title meant for players seeking fast, arcade-style action or modern production values. Instead, it rewards those who embrace slow, strategic gameplay and appreciate simulations that strive for authenticity over spectacle. Its vast environments, immersive atmosphere, and uncompromising design philosophy still resonate today, offering an experience that feels raw, deliberate, and surprisingly timeless. For fans of military strategy or anyone interested in the roots of the Arma series, Cold War Assault is more than a classic—it’s a foundational chapter in the evolution of realistic shooters.

This isn't a run-and-gun game! You have to plan things out, and sometimes things won't go according to plan; you're a squishy human being who will die in one or two shots. But this makes victory all the more satisfying, and fortunately, your enemies share this same weakness, making it way more realistic than any other shooter released at the time. 

And there's the editor... oh boy, this made me feel like I was playing with plastic toy soldiers again; you have the ability to create your own scenarios, giving you the ability to make your own fun. Unfortunately for those who have played ArmA 2 and ArmA 3, you won't find the editor that great. It's easy to notice what features weren't around when Operation Flashpoint came out. Init fields, special fields, elevation, name fields, modules, and many more features aren't present here. But that just comes to show how far the series has come, and if it weren't for this starting point, we wouldn't have the impressive editor we have in ArmA 3 currently.

I still remember the day I installed this on my first PC back in 2009. The moment that soldier’s eyes locked onto mine from the cover, I knew I was in for something special. This wasn’t just a game—it was my battlefield, my playground, my obsession. I played it endlessly, year after year, until 2017. The gritty realism, the tactical depth, the Cold War tension—it all felt larger than life. And that soundtrack? Pure magic. It echoed through my room like a war hymn, making every mission feel like a movie scene.
Now in 2026, I'm downloading it again, chasing that feeling. Some games age, but this one? It became part of my story. If you were a kid back then, you know exactly what I mean.

Some games are more than just games. They’re memories you can never truly leave behind.

I grew up in a military housing complex, and the only video rental shop in the area mostly carried war games. I was only five or six years old when I picked up this game. I didn’t even know its name back then. All I knew was that it felt incredibly exciting, fascinating, and, honestly, ridiculously difficult for a kid my age!

I absolutely loved the idea of getting into a tank and driving around, or simply exploring the map with no particular objective in mind. I didn’t need to understand every mechanic or complete every mission. Just being there, discovering the world, and messing around was enough to make my day.

Then, one day, the game disc stopped working. I couldn’t remember the title, and just like that, the game disappeared from my life. For years, I couldn’t find it again. I kept wishing I could play it one more time, without even knowing whether I’d ever get the chance.

And now? It’s sitting right here in my Steam library. After all those years of searching and wondering, I finally found it again. The funny thing is, I might not even feel like playing it that much anymore. Maybe I’ve changed. Maybe the game hasn’t aged as well as I remember. Or maybe some things are simply better left untouched, preserved exactly as they were in our childhood memories.

But that’s not really the point.

I just wanted to share this little piece of my childhood and remind you of something: cherish the moments you have while you’re living them. Enjoy the games, the people, and the little things that make you happy today. Because sometimes, years later, you’ll realize that what you miss most isn’t the thing itself, but the person you were when you first experienced it.

You never know which ordinary moment will become a precious memory, or which game you’ll spend years trying to find again.

So live in the moment. Enjoy it while it lasts. You only get to experience your childhood once.

I wanted to give this game a fair shot, since it is essentially the start of the Arma franchise. After seeing the main campaign through to the end (I can't say anything for the standalone missions, the mission editor, or the multiplayer), I cannot say I enjoyed the majority of my time with it. About 7 hours of my playtime was me having fun. The rest was sheer frustration and annoyance.

To start off, there are four main types of play styles in the campaign: standard infantry combat, tank combat, aerial vehicles (primarily helicopters), and stealth-based missions. These four aren't mutually exclusive, as getting seen while sneaking will obviously turn things into a firefight, and the late game provides the infantry with all sorts of land and aerial vehicles to use at their disposal. After getting the hang of the controls, I found the tank gameplay to be the most consistently enjoyable. There is just something innately satisfying about driving straight through the Soviet lines and blasting apart anything that tries to shoot you. The only real issue I had here was sometimes the driver AI would just start driving off in the complete opposite direction from where I ordered him, but even in the worst-case scenarios, this could be remedied by immediately swapping to the driver's seat with the push of a button.

The infantry combat could also be fun at times, but it is also the one that suffers the most from the game's issues. For starters, the game does a horrible job teaching the player key components of gameplay before thrusting them into a firefight. The tutorial teaches you the bare minimum: how to move, shoot, and reload. It fails to mention anything about aiming down the sights, a vital component for actually hitting anything more than 20 meters away from you. It fails to discuss how to use any of the secondary weapons, meaning when you do acquire one, using it is up to trial and error. When the radio and squad mechanic is introduced, you are given no explanation as to what most of the options actually mean, so you have to issue an order to the squad and hope it means what you think it does; otherwise, your soldiers are lambs for the Soviets to slaughter.

Speaking of the AI, even if you do understand what orders to give them, there is no guarantee that the AI will actually follow them like they should. "Take cover" usually means finding something solid to hide behind, or at least hitting the dirt to minimize your size. But some soldiers take it to mean "charge the enemy across an open field." Other times, the AI will stare an enemy soldier in the eyes and suddenly become a pacifist, refusing to fire a shot even as a Soviet turns him into Swiss cheese. Sometimes your allies will have startlingly good accuracy, nailing enemies hundreds of meters away, but other times they resemble Stormtroopers with their accuracy. Very often, you will give your squad orders to move to a specific location, but they will try to go the most meandering, roundabout way to get there, if they even get there at all. The game introduces a "tactical view" mode, or something of the sort, to help micromanage your troops for, say, defending a position or staging an ambush, but it really doesn't tell you anything more than that it exists, so I could not really use it to to my benefit at all. When the AI works properly and everything falls into place, these make for some of the best moments of the game. Seeing enemy after enemy drop from bursts of rifle fire and hearing "enemy soldier is history" over the radio chatter is very satisfying, but it is only some moments this happens. Most often, the AI will find some way to screw up your plans, making each firefight more of a hassle than it needs to be.

As for flying a helicopter, the controls are actually fairly well-explained. The default key mapping may not be the most natural, but it wasn't a big issue. The only thing I truly struggled with was accurately landing my helicopter, as I'd always land a few hundred meters away from where I intended to touch down (this may also just have been a "me" problem, not something inherent to the game). On the other hand, combat with the helicopter was an absolute trainwreck. Most of the helicopters have three types of weapons: a machine gun, homing missiles, and unguided missiles. The AI gunner will NEVER hit anything with its machine gun, even stationary targets. No matter how I positioned my helicopter, he would always overshoot and miss the target. As for the lock-on missiles, the homing functionality is again not reliable, even on stationary targets, and especially not on moving ones. These are particularly frustrating since your helicopter will be armed with, at most, 8 missiles, which will have to last you for the whole mission. The unguided missiles are very unwieldy to aim, since you need to point the nose of your chopper at the ground target and then score a direct hit with the missiles. Since pointing your nose at the ground means your chopper will be accelerating, it may take several passes and over a dozen rockets just to take down a single tank.

Finally, there's the stealth missions. A lot of the same problems as the infantry section apply here, but with the added caveat of questionable stealth mechanics. Sometimes you can be basically right on top of an enemy (within 20 meters) and they still won't see you. Other times you will be spotted while prone from over 200 meters away. Sometimes the whole base will be alerted without any indication that you did something wrong. But the most frustrating part is the game's "needle in a haystack" approach to having you achieve the objective. The game reminds me a lot of the early Hitman games in that yes, the level is open for you to try a bunch of different things to meet your objective, but there's really only one arbitrary, "correct" way that will actually work, and the only way you to find that out is trial and error, an issue compounded by the game's horrible checkpoint system. The checkpoint system and the slow pace of the stealth levels means each attempt can be upwards of 10 minutes, often of little more than crawling on your stomach for hundreds or even thousands of meters. Not helping this fact is that the game's "suggestions" will actually hurt more than help. "Try destroying the AA vehicles one at a time!" Except after the first one is destroyed, the other two are alerted and start moving, making it impossible to plant bombs on them. "Instead of silently killing the guards at the base's front gate, blow a hole in the fence!" Thanks, now the entire base, including 5 armored vehicles and dozens of guards, are alerted and are converging on my position.

I don't want to be entirely negative. There were a few things I did genuinely enjoy. Like I said, the tank sections and moments of the infantry combat clicked with me and were enjoyable. The core idea is fairly interesting, since not too many FPS games go for the late Cold War aesthetic, where both American and Soviet weapons were sophisticated, advanced, and designed to counter one another. The premise is also great: a forgotten conflict on a seemingly random island that could have easily boiled over into World War III, but was stopped thanks to the success of the protagonists. Also, the scope of the conflict is presented well, since you see the same areas of the map in different contexts as the war progresses. A town you failed to defend from the Soviets may later be used by them to fuel and repair their helicopters. Your tank offensive fails because of anti-armor emplacements, so your infantry squad in the next mission is sent to eliminate them. Of course, the best of this is in the aerial levels, where those villages you fought to capture, level-by-level, all come together on this large island, making it feel like you've truly made progress in pushing back the invasion, regaining the kilometers you once lost.

ARMA: Cold War Assault is an awesome game. I was hoping to be able to finish the bundled DLC before reviewing the game, but it's fiendishly difficult and so I gave up, but the base game is fantastic if you like realistic first-person shooters.

I picked this game up when Russia invaded Ukraine (again), mainly because the game's campaign is based on essentially exactly that storyline. I am a fan of "one shot kills" first-person shooters and slow-paced/stealth games, and this game has a similar feel to it, plus vehicles and giant maps. I always knew of Arma 3 as being a "serious" military sim with a strong multiplayer and modding community, but I had no idea the first game also included a compelling single-player campaign.

You play the role of a couple of different soldiers defending a fictional East European country from a Russian invasion, and although each mission has clear goals and predefined strategies, it's also an open world that allows you to achieve the objectives in all manner of off-the-wall ways. This is a very old game so the vehicles in particular are prone to bugs and jank, but if your tank gets stuck in a wall occasionally you can still jump out, go prone, crawl around the whole map trying to find another vehicle or anti-tank weapon, then come back and take out your target and still finish the mission. And when you succeed in that kind of ridiculous save it feels amazing, because it's actually incredibly difficult to pull off, even if you do figure out ways to cheese some of the enemy AI. You can die very, very easily in this game, and that makes it so much more tense than shooters where you and everyone else is a bullet sponge. At the end of the campaign you get to meet up with a bunch of your squaddies and it really feels like you went through a war together - I literally teared up!

As mentioned earlier, the DLC is especially difficult, because a similar invasion storyline happens, but you are just a regular joe on the way to work. The campaign starts with you jumping on your motorcycle while the tanks roll in, and then you need to escape into the forest and set up a resistance unit keeping only the weapons and vehicles your team can salvage from mission to mission. I wish I could have completed it because it sounds like a fantastic storyline, but it's hard. This whole game is hard. Hard, but rewarding. If you want to play a fairly realistic military shooter from the last age of warfare before drones changed the game, you could do a lot worse than this.

One point I would stress is that the infantry experience is much better than the vehicles experience. In the main campaign by far the most frustrating missions are the ones where you need to drive a tank or fly a chopper to complete some timed objective. Usually with infantry-centric missions you can lean on your AI squadmates to back you up through tight spots, but with vehicles all bets are off. On the other hand, having vehicles on the battlefield does make it feel more realistic, and makes it even easier to get killed as PBI, which just ratchets up the tension further. Man, even just thinking back to my playthrough a year later has me thrilled. I think I might go wishlist Arma 2.

The fact they have remastered the renderer, released the source code, and have made several improvements has been honestly a little shocking. A great unexpected surprise for me. This has been an amazing upgrade. I also no longer experience a very annoying mouse acceleration bug that was plaguing me previously. The fact they released this free for existing owners is also really awesome of Bohemia. The 64-bit conversion has been fantastic, and I wish they could update every other Arma to 64 bit now, but I will take what I can get. The game still can be very immersive if you are in the right headspace for it, and overall it still has my favorite campaigns of the whole franchise. Highly recommended to give it a shot if it's been a while since you have a played it or if you are new to the franchise as a whole. See how it all started!

What a game! I played this over 10 years ago and the gameplay is just as good today. Back then it was called Operation Flashpoint - Cold War Crisis, from 2001 but due to copyright issues it has been renamed under the ARMA brand in 2011.

This game is a war/army simulator and as such it is bound under certain simulation rules. For example everything is hard as balls to operate. Tanks, helicopters, boats ... and planes, holy hell is it difficult to fly planes! But once you learn it, it is fantastic! Flying around in an Apache helicopter and raining hell down on all those shiny tanks is AWESOME! All this is present in the single missions but mainly the campaign.

The campaign does give you missions and an outline on how to do them. But you can just ignore all that and do a lot of the stuff your own way! Place C4 to destroy 4 tanks? Nah, get in one of the tanks and wreck everything (including low flying choppers) instead! Carefully use stealth to get to the extraction point while avoiding BMPs and patroling soldiers? Nope, just steal a Skoda 120 car and zig zag between the tank and soldier fire! Examples like these is what made the game great for me.

What extends the experience even more is the missions you do yourself in the editor. However there are downsides too - graphical glitches, stupid AI sometimes and cardboard graphics. Multiplayer is pretty much dead except for LAN. But if you manage to hook up a MP game with some friend(s) you will not regret it. Yes, it is a bit laggy because the network code is rubbish, but it still is loads of fun. I recommend this retro game that despite the flaws is just so much fun!
